Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW YORK (CNN) -- Federal, state and municipal agencies staged an elaborate drill in the waters off New York City on Tuesday to prepare for the possibility of a nuclear or dirty-bomb attack from the water. A U.S. Coast Guard vessel passes a container ship in New York Harbor as part of Tuesday's terror drill. "We're a big city, and there are vulnerabilities," said Ray Kelly, commissioner of the New York Police Department. Agencies involved in Tuesday's test  emphasized they did not undertake it because of a specific threat against the city. However, Kelly said the city was taking no chances after a proclamation years ago by Osama bin Laden. "We do know that Osama bin Laden several years ago obtained a fatwah to use nuclear weapons, and our goal is to make certain that that fatwah does not come to fruition," he said. In addition to increasing various agencies' preparedness for a seaborne radiological attack, Kelly said Tuesday's well-publicized drill was meant to deter those who would perpetrate such an attack. "It pays to advertise to a certain extent. We want anyone who would do us harm to know that we're out there, that we have the capability to detect," Kelly said. Eight government agencies participated in the drill, ranging from the NYPD to the U.S. Coast Guard. The exercise took place at the entrance of New York Harbor, just south of the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge linking Staten Island to Brooklyn. Per the drill's plan, eight boats were to cross a checkpoint set up by authorities. They were on the lookout for abnormally high concentrations of radioactivity -- a telltale sign of an improvised nuclear device or a radiological dispersal device, more familiarly known as a dirty bomb. Some of the boats were decoys with no radioactive substances aboard, while others had actual radioactive isotopes planted in them. A radioactivity detector in the hull of the authorities' boats was to identify which vessels had radioactive substances in them. The devices are highly sensitive -- so much so that people who have recently had certain medical treatments can set them off. It was up to the authorities participating in the drill to sort the good boats from the bad -- and to intercept the bad. Only minutes into the six-hour exercise, equipment aboard a police boat detected radioactivity within a small white pleasure craft passing through the checkpoint. Two patrol vessels then converged on the pleasure craft, while officials began to question the driver and his two passengers. Soon after, authorities boarded the boat and used a radiation detector, officially known as a radiological isotope identification detector, to produce a "spectrum" of the radiological material. They then transmitted the spectrum to the Department of Homeland Security's Joint Analysis Center (JAC) in Washington to determine precisely what radiological material was aboard the boat. Within moments, the JAC radioed back with a positive identification: Caesium-137, an industrial radioactive isotope that if used in large enough quantities could power a devastating dirty bomb. Sure enough, when a separate boat containing press and police officers sidled up to the apprehended craft soon afterward, the portable radioactivity detectors of officers onboard began to sound excitedly. NYPD Sgt. Art Mogil said that, in part, the agencies chose to practice on leisure craft to illustrate that radiological weapons could be transported in deceptively benign-looking boats. "It doesn't require a large vessel. A device can be just a few pounds and still be a major threat," Mogil said. James Waters, counterterrorism chief for the NYPD, said exercises like Tuesday's were vital because the stakes involved are so high. "Someone bringing in a radiological or nuclear device would be very serious if not catastrophic," he said. On an average day, not all incoming maritime traffic in New York City is subjected to the radioactivity tests performed at Tuesday's drill. An NYPD official declined to specify what percentage of boats normally undergo such screening.

A U.S. Coast Guard vessel passes a container ship in New York Harbor as part of Tuesday's terror drill.

"We're a big city, and there are vulnerabilities," said Ray Kelly, commissioner of the New York Police Department.

The agencies involved in Tuesday's exercise emphasized that it was not prompted by any specific threat against the city. Nevertheless, Kelly noted that authorities were taking no chances, citing a proclamation issued years earlier by Osama bin Laden. "We do know that Osama bin Laden several years ago obtained a fatwa to use nuclear weapons, and our goal is to ensure that fatwa never comes to fruition," he said.

Beyond enhancing various agencies' readiness for a seaborne radiological attack, Kelly explained that Tuesday's highly publicized drill was also designed to serve as a deterrent to potential perpetrators. "It pays to advertise, to a certain extent. We want anyone who would do us harm to know that we're out there, and that we have the capability to detect such threats," Kelly said.

Eight government agencies took part in the exercise, ranging from the NYPD to the U.S. Coast Guard. It was conducted at the entrance to New York Harbor, just south of the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge connecting Staten Island to Brooklyn.

According to the drill's design, eight boats were to pass through a checkpoint established by authorities, who monitored for abnormally high concentrations of radioactivity—a telltale indicator of an improvised nuclear device or a radiological dispersal device, more commonly known as a dirty bomb. Some boats served as decoys, carrying no radioactive material, while others had genuine radioactive isotopes planted aboard. A radioactivity detector installed in the hull of the authorities' vessels was used to distinguish which boats carried radioactive substances.

These devices are extraordinarily sensitive—so much so that individuals who have recently undergone certain medical treatments can inadvertently trigger them. It fell to the participating authorities to differentiate the legitimate vessels from the suspect ones—and to intercept the latter.

Just minutes into the six-hour exercise, equipment aboard a police boat detected radioactivity emanating from a small white pleasure craft passing through the checkpoint. Two patrol vessels swiftly converged on the boat, and officials began questioning the driver and his two passengers. Shortly thereafter, authorities boarded the craft and employed a radiation detector—formally known as a radiological isotope identification device—to generate a "spectrum" of the radiological material present.

This spectrum was then transmitted to the Department of Homeland Security's Joint Analysis Center (JAC) in Washington for precise identification of the radiological material aboard. Within moments, the JAC responded with a positive identification: Cesium-137, an industrial radioactive isotope capable of powering a devastating dirty bomb if present in sufficient quantities.

Sure enough, when a separate boat carrying press and police officers approached the apprehended craft shortly afterward, the portable radioactivity detectors carried by officers aboard began sounding urgently.

NYPD Sgt. Art Mogil explained that the agencies had, in part, chosen to test leisure craft specifically to demonstrate that radiological weapons could be transported aboard deceptively innocuous-looking boats. "It doesn't require a large vessel. A device can weigh just a few pounds and still pose a major threat," Mogil said.

James Waters, the NYPD's counterterrorism chief, emphasized that exercises like Tuesday's are essential given the extraordinarily high stakes involved. "Someone bringing in a radiological or nuclear device would be very serious, if not catastrophic," he said.

NEW YORK (CNN) -- On Tuesday, multiple government agencies representing federal, state, and city levels conducted a sophisticated training exercise in New York City's harbor to test readiness against a potential nuclear or radiological weapon smuggled in by boat.

A Coast Guard ship was seen passing a cargo vessel in the harbor during the exercise. "Given our size as a major metropolis, certain weaknesses exist," explained NYPD Commissioner Ray Kelly.

Officials from the participating agencies stressed that the exercise wasn't prompted by any known imminent threat. Nevertheless, Kelly noted that the city remained vigilant in light of a past declaration by Osama bin Laden.

"We're aware that Osama bin Laden issued a religious edict years back authorizing the use of nuclear weapons, and we're committed to preventing that edict from ever being carried out," Kelly stated.

Beyond sharpening the response capabilities of various agencies against a maritime radiological threat, Kelly explained that publicizing Tuesday's exercise served as a warning to potential attackers. "There's value in making this known publicly. We want potential attackers to understand that we maintain constant vigilance and possess detection capabilities," he noted.

The training brought together eight separate government bodies, including the NYPD and the Coast Guard. The location chosen was the harbor's entry point, situated just below the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge connecting Staten Island and Brooklyn.

According to the exercise design, eight vessels were scheduled to pass through a security checkpoint established by officials, who watched for elevated radiation levels—an indicator of either a homemade nuclear device or what's commonly termed a dirty bomb. Several boats served as decoys carrying no radioactive material, whereas others had genuine radioactive isotopes placed aboard. Radiation sensors built into the hulls of the monitoring vessels were designed to distinguish which boats carried radioactive cargo. These instruments possess remarkable sensitivity, capable of triggering alerts even from individuals who've undergone certain recent medical procedures.

The challenge for exercise participants involved correctly identifying and stopping the vessels carrying radioactive material.

Within mere minutes of the exercise's six-hour duration, sensors on a police vessel picked up radiation signals emanating from a small white recreational boat passing through the checkpoint. Two patrol boats immediately moved to surround the craft, while officers began questioning its operator and two passengers.

Authorities subsequently boarded the vessel, employing a specialized instrument called a radiological isotope identification detector to generate a radiation "signature." This data was then relayed to the Joint Analysis Center (JAC), part of the Department of Homeland Security based in Washington, for precise identification of the radioactive substance.

The JAC quickly responded with confirmation: the material was Caesium-137, an industrial-grade radioactive isotope capable of fueling a serious dirty bomb if present in sufficient quantity. This finding was corroborated shortly after when a separate boat carrying journalists and police personnel approached the detained craft—portable radiation detectors carried by officers aboard immediately began signaling detection.

NYPD Sergeant Art Mogil explained that recreational boats were deliberately selected for part of the exercise to demonstrate how radiological weapons could be concealed within seemingly harmless watercraft. "You don't need a large boat for this. Even a device weighing just a few pounds can pose a serious danger," Mogil noted.

James Waters, who heads counterterrorism efforts for the NYPD, emphasized the critical importance of such exercises given the severe potential consequences. "The introduction of a radiological or nuclear device would represent an extremely serious, potentially catastrophic scenario," he said.

Currently, not every vessel entering New York's waters undergoes the radiation screening demonstrated in Tuesday's exercise. When asked, an NYPD spokesperson would not disclose what proportion of maritime traffic typically receives such scrutiny.

Federal, state, and municipal agencies came together recently to conduct an elaborate security drill in New York Harbor, simulating a scenario in which terrorists might attempt to smuggle a nuclear device or radiological "dirty bomb" into the city by water. The exercise represented a significant coordinated effort to test and refine the region's ability to detect and respond to one of the most feared forms of terrorist attack.

**Multi-Agency Drill Tests NYC's Defenses Against Nuclear, Radiological Threats From the Water**

*Officials say exercise reflects growing concern over maritime approaches to major U.S. ports*

NEW YORK — Small boats bristling with radiation sensors crisscrossed New York Harbor this week as federal, state and local agencies staged a large-scale drill designed to test the region's ability to detect a nuclear device or "dirty bomb" smuggled in by water.

The exercise, which unfolded over several days across the harbor and its approaches, brought together the Coast Guard, the NYPD, the Department of Energy's National Nuclear Security Administration, and Customs and Border Protection, according to officials familiar with the operation. Helicopters equipped with radiological detection equipment flew low over the water while dive teams and vessels patrolled shipping lanes near the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, the Statue of Liberty and container terminals in New Jersey.

"This is one of the most complex maritime environments in the world, and it's also one of the most attractive targets," said one federal law enforcement official involved in planning the drill, who spoke on condition of anonymity because details of the exercise are sensitive. "You have cruise ships, ferries, tankers, container vessels — all moving through a very tight space. We have to be able to find a threat in that noise."

The scenario, according to officials briefed on the exercise, involved simulated intelligence suggesting that radioactive material — potentially usable in a crude nuclear device or a so-called dirty bomb, which pairs conventional explosives with radioactive material to spread contamination — had entered U.S. waters aboard a commercial vessel or small craft. Teams practiced tracking, boarding and screening procedures without disrupting the flow of commercial traffic, one of the trickiest aspects of harbor security given that thousands of containers move through the Port of New York and New Jersey each day.

The drill is part of a broader, largely unpublicized effort by the Department of Homeland Security and its partners to harden American ports against radiological and nuclear threats, a priority that has taken on renewed urgency amid concerns about smuggling routes, aging Soviet-era nuclear stockpiles, and the proliferation of dirty bomb components on the black market.

"Nuclear terrorism remains a low-probability, high-consequence threat," said a former DHS official who has worked on port security issues but was not authorized to discuss the specific exercise. "But because the consequences are so catastrophic, the government has to keep pressure-testing its systems, even in a city like New York that already has multiple layers of protection."

New York Harbor is considered a uniquely difficult environment to secure. It spans hundreds of miles of shoreline across two states, includes some of the busiest passenger and cargo terminals in the country, and sits beneath one of the most densely populated urban areas in the world. Radiation portal monitors already screen cargo at major terminals, and the NYPD has long operated a radiological detection unit as part of its counterterrorism operations, but officials say water-based threats present distinct challenges because small boats can bypass fixed checkpoints.

The NYPD's Counterterrorism Bureau, which has participated in similar exercises in the past, referred questions about this week's drill to federal authorities. The Coast Guard confirmed it took part in a "routine training exercise" in the harbor but declined to discuss specifics, citing security concerns.

Neither the Coast Guard nor DHS indicated the drill was in response to a specific or credible threat. Officials characterized it instead as part of an ongoing, recurring effort to test detection technology, refine coordination between agencies, and train personnel — exercises that have become more frequent in major coastal cities since the September 11 attacks.

Still, the timing drew attention. The drill comes amid broader concerns among U.S. intelligence agencies about the security of nuclear material overseas and the potential for it to be trafficked through commercial shipping networks, concerns that have periodically surfaced in congressional hearings and government watchdog reports over the past decade.

For now, officials say, the exercise underscores a sobering reality of homeland security in a global port city: much of the work happens quietly, on the water, far from public view — and is designed to stay that way unless something goes wrong.

CNN has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security and the NYPD for additional comment.

The training operation involved the U.S. Coast Guard, Customs and Border Protection, the New York Police Department's harbor and counterterrorism units, and representatives from the Department of Energy's radiological response teams, according to officials familiar with the exercise.

Small boat teams practiced approaching and boarding simulated target vessels, while personnel used handheld and vessel-mounted radiation detection equipment to screen cargo and hulls.

Coast Guard cutters and NYPD harbor patrol boats worked in coordination with fixed radiation portal monitors, similar to those already in use at some port facilities, to test layered detection strategies across different points of entry into the harbor.

"Exercises like this allow us to identify gaps in our detection network and improve coordination between agencies that would need to respond in a real incident," said a Coast Guard spokesperson, who described the training as part of ongoing efforts to secure critical maritime infrastructure in the region.

## Broader Context

New York Harbor, one of the busiest ports on the East Coast, has long been considered a potential vulnerability given the volume of commercial and recreational traffic passing through its waters daily. Security officials have periodically conducted similar exercises since the early 2000s as part of broader efforts to guard against nuclear or radiological terrorism.

The Domestic Nuclear Detection Office and other federal partners have previously supported similar drills in major U.S. ports, emphasizing detection technology, inter-agency communication, and rapid response protocols.

Officials did not disclose the exact locations or timing of follow-up exercises, citing security concerns, but indicated that similar training would continue on a recurring basis.

# Multi-Agency Security Drill Near Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge Tests Response to Maritime Terror Threat

**NEW YORK** — Coast Guard cutters sliced through the choppy waters beneath the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge Wednesday morning as NYPD helicopters circled overhead, part of a large-scale joint security exercise designed to test how quickly law enforcement agencies could respond to a coordinated terrorist attack targeting one of the region's critical infrastructure points.

The drill, conducted jointly by the New York Police Department, the U.S. Coast Guard, and the Department of Homeland Security, simulated a scenario in which a small vessel loaded with explosives attempted to approach the bridge's support towers — a threat scenario security officials have studied closely since the 2000 USS Cole bombing in Yemen demonstrated the destructive potential of small watercraft.

"We cannot afford to wait for an attack to test our capabilities," former NYPD Commissioner Raymond Kelly said at a press briefing following the exercise. "New York remains the number one terrorist target in the United States, and this bridge, this harbor, represents exactly the kind of high-profile infrastructure that our adversaries have shown interest in over the years. Today's exercise allows us to identify gaps before they're exploited, not after."

The exercise involved roughly a dozen vessels, including NYPD Harbor Unit boats, Coast Guard response cutters, and DHS-coordinated support craft, alongside aerial surveillance assets. Officials said the drill tested communication protocols between agencies, response times, and the ability to establish a security perimeter around the bridge on short notice.

"Interagency coordination is the backbone of maritime domain security," said a Coast Guard sector commander involved in the planning. "A bridge like the Verrazzano isn't just a piece of infrastructure — it's a chokepoint for both the harbor and the region's transportation network. If something happens there, the ripple effects hit the entire metropolitan area."

The Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, connecting Staten Island and Brooklyn, has long been considered a potential target due to its symbolic value and its role as the gateway to New York Harbor. It also marks the starting point of the New York City Marathon, drawing tens of thousands of spectators annually — a factor officials say adds another layer of urgency to securing the span.

DHS officials emphasized that the exercise was part of a broader, ongoing effort to harden security around the nation's bridges, tunnels, and waterways, particularly in the years following the September 11 attacks reshaped federal approaches to critical infrastructure protection.

"These drills aren't for show," a DHS spokesperson said. "They generate real data — response times, communication gaps, procedural bottlenecks — that feed directly into how we allocate resources and refine protocols going forward."

Kelly, who has overseen numerous counterterrorism initiatives during his tenure, noted that the NYPD's Harbor Unit and its broader counterterrorism apparatus have expanded significantly, incorporating intelligence-sharing agreements with federal partners and increased patrols around sensitive waterways.

"We've built one of the most sophisticated counterterrorism operations of any police department in the world," Kelly said. "But sophistication means nothing if we don't stress-test it constantly against realistic scenarios."

Local officials and maritime traffic controllers said the exercise caused only minor disruptions to harbor traffic, with advisories issued in advance to commercial shippers and ferry operators.

Security experts say exercises like Wednesday's reflect a broader shift in post-9/11 policing, in which visible, large-scale drills serve both a practical and deterrent function.

"There's an operational value and there's a psychological value," said one former federal counterterrorism official not involved in organizing the drill. "You want potential attackers to see that this isn't a soft target — that agencies are watching, coordinating, and ready to respond within minutes, not hours."

Officials declined to specify how frequently such drills are conducted, citing security concerns, but indicated that similar exercises are held periodically at other high-value sites throughout the city's five boroughs, including other East River and Hudson River crossings.

As the exercise wound down Wednesday afternoon, vessels returned to their berths and normal harbor traffic resumed. Officials said an after-action report evaluating the drill's findings would be compiled in the coming weeks, with recommendations expected to shape future training and resource allocation.

"This is a continuous process," Kelly said. "The threat evolves, so our preparedness has to evolve right alongside it."

Officials pointed to longstanding intelligence concerns about al-Qaeda's nuclear ambitions as part of the rationale behind continued investment in the program. Analysts have long cited a 1998 declaration attributed to Osama bin Laden, in which he framed the acquisition of weapons of mass destruction—including nuclear, chemical, and biological weapons—as a religious obligation, describing it as a duty incumbent upon Muslims to counter what he called Western aggression. Bin Laden reiterated this position in subsequent statements, and captured al-Qaeda documents and detainee interrogations after 2001 indicated the group had explored acquiring radioactive material, though experts differ on how far those efforts progressed.

"The fatwa language from the late 1990s made clear that acquiring these capabilities wasn't viewed as a last resort but as a strategic goal," said Dr. Elena Marchetti, a nonproliferation researcher at a Washington think tank who has studied the group's WMD ambitions. "Even after bin Laden's death, that ideological framework didn't disappear. It's part of why cities like New York maintain persistent detection infrastructure rather than treating this as a one-time risk."

The Securing the Cities program, launched in 2003 following congressional appropriations tied to post-9/11 preparedness, has expanded radiation detection equipment across the New York metropolitan region, including bridges, tunnels, and rail hubs in addition to maritime approaches. Similar frameworks have since been adopted in other major U.S. metropolitan areas, including Los Angeles and Chicago.

This week's exercise also included interagency coordination with the Department of Energy's National Nuclear Security Administration, whose Radiological Assistance Program teams provided technical support and helped calibrate detection thresholds against a range of simulated source materials.

Officials declined to detail specific detection technologies or thresholds, citing operational security concerns, but emphasized that exercises like this week's are conducted multiple times per year, often without public announcement.

"The goal is to make this routine enough that our response capability doesn't degrade, but varied enough that it can't be studied and defeated," the NYPD official said. "We don't get a second chance to get this right."

The exercise concluded Thursday with a tabletop debrief involving representatives from the Coast Guard, NYPD, FDNY, and DHS, according to a statement released by the mayor's office.

# Multi-Agency Exercise Tests Radiological Detection Capabilities in New York Harbor

**NEW YORK** — In a coordinated training exercise conducted last week, federal, state, and local agencies simulated the detection and response to a radiological threat aboard maritime vessels navigating New York Harbor, testing the region's layered defense systems against potential nuclear or radiological terrorism.

## Exercise Overview

The drill, conducted under the Department of Homeland Security's Securing the Cities program in coordination with the U.S. Coast Guard, New York Police Department, and Customs and Border Protection, involved multiple vessels transiting through harbor approaches near the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge and up the Hudson and East Rivers. Officials said the exercise was designed without advance notice to patrol units in order to test real-world response times and detection accuracy.

Participating agencies deployed a mix of **decoy vessels**—carrying no radioactive material—alongside a small number of boats loaded with **low-activity check sources**, commonly used isotopes that mimic the radiological signature of materials that could theoretically be used in a "dirty bomb" or improvised nuclear device without posing any actual public health risk.

## Technical Detection Methods

According to officials familiar with the exercise, the test sources included small quantities of **Cesium-137, Cobalt-60, and Americium-241**, isotopes chosen because their gamma-ray emission signatures are frequently referenced in threat scenarios and are used in industrial, medical, and calibration equipment.

- **Cesium-137** emits gamma rays at approximately 662 keV, a signature commonly associated with contamination scenarios and stolen medical equipment.
- **Cobalt-60**, used widely in radiotherapy and industrial radiography, emits higher-energy gammas at 1.17 and 1.33 MeV, making it detectable at greater distances but also more challenging to shield.
- **Americium-241**, found in smoke detectors and industrial gauges, emits lower-energy gamma and alpha radiation, testing the sensitivity thresholds of shipborne and handheld detectors.

Coast Guard vessels equipped with **Radiation Isotope Identification Devices (RIIDs)** and Personal Radiation Detectors (PRDs) patrolled alongside NYPD's Harbor Unit, which has integrated radiological detection into its fleet since the mid-2000s. Backup detection was provided by CBP's Radiation Portal Monitors positioned near cargo terminals, cross-referencing harbor traffic against manifests.

The NYPD's Counterterrorism Bureau, which operates a network of fixed and mobile detectors as part of its broader "Domain Awareness System," also fielded units carrying backpack-style detectors capable of relaying isotope identification data in real time to a central command post.

## Agency Coordination and Response Protocol

Officials say the exercise emphasized **detection-to-decision timelines**—the interval between initial alarm, secondary confirmation, isotope identification, and vessel interdiction.

"When a detector alarms, the first priority is determining whether we're looking at a naturally occurring radioactive material, a medical isotope from a patient who recently underwent treatment, or something that requires immediate escalation," said one federal official granted anonymity to discuss operational details. "Speed matters, but so does accuracy — false positives erode public trust and operational tempo."

Once a detection occurred, protocol called for Coast Guard small boat units to establish a safety perimeter while NYPD Emergency Service Unit teams equipped with additional identification equipment moved to confirm readings. Simulated communications were relayed to the Joint Terrorism Task Force and a mock Incident Command Post established onshore, testing information-sharing pathways between agencies that don't typically operate under unified command.

## Broader Context

New York Harbor has been considered a priority area for radiological detection since the Securing the Cities initiative launched in 2007, given the density of maritime traffic, critical infrastructure, and population centers within a compact geographic radius. The program has since expanded to other major urban areas but retains its most mature architecture in the New York region.

Federal officials declined to specify exact dates or precise locations of future exercises, citing operational security concerns, but confirmed that similar drills occur multiple times annually, often incorporating updated detection technology and evolving threat scenarios based on intelligence assessments.

"These exercises aren't about achieving perfection in a single afternoon," the federal official said. "They're about building institutional muscle memory so that when seconds matter, agencies aren't meeting each other for the first time."

No public safety concerns were associated with the exercise, and harbor traffic was not disrupted beyond routine patrol patterns.
